before.content_html:
What Is a Force?

A force is a push or a pull that acts on an object. Forces are measured in newtons (N). Every force arises because two objects are interacting — either by touching or at a distance.

Contact forces act when objects are physically in contact. Examples include friction, normal contact force, tension, and air resistance. Non-contact forces act at a distance through fields — gravitational force, electrostatic force, and magnetic force are all non-contact forces.

Key Fact

Forces always come in pairs. When two objects interact, each exerts a force on the other. These interaction pairs can be represented as vectors.

Scalars and Vectors

A scalar quantity has magnitude only. A vector quantity has both magnitude and direction. Force is a vector — it has a size and acts in a particular direction. Mass is a scalar — it has only size.

Key vector quantities include displacement, velocity, acceleration, force, and momentum. Key scalar quantities include distance, speed, mass, energy, and temperature.

A free body diagram shows all the forces acting on a single object. Each force is drawn as an arrow starting from the object. The length of the arrow represents the size of the force, and the direction of the arrow shows which way the force acts.

When the arrows are equal and opposite, the forces are balanced and the resultant force is zero. When they are unequal, there is a net (resultant) force and the object will accelerate.

Newton's First Law

Newton's first law states that if the resultant force acting on an object is zero, the object will remain stationary or continue to move at a constant velocity in a straight line. If the resultant force is not zero, the object will accelerate — its speed or direction (or both) will change.

Key Fact

An object moving at constant velocity has a resultant force of zero. It does not need a force to keep it moving — only to change its motion.

Newton's Second Law

Newton's second law tells us that the acceleration of an object is directly proportional to the resultant force and inversely proportional to its mass. The equation is:

$$F = m \times a$$

where \(F\) is the resultant force in newtons (N), \(m\) is the mass in kilograms (kg), and \(a\) is the acceleration in metres per second squared (m/s²).

Weight is the force of gravity acting on an object. It is a vector quantity measured in newtons using a newton meter (spring balance). The equation is:

$$W = m \times g$$

where \(W\) is weight in newtons (N), \(m\) is mass in kilograms (kg), and \(g\) is the gravitational field strength in N/kg. On Earth, \(g \approx 9.8\) N/kg.

Mass is a scalar — it stays the same everywhere. Weight is a vector — it changes depending on the gravitational field strength.

Newton's Third Law

Newton's third law states that whenever two objects interact, they exert equal and opposite forces on each other. These forces act on different objects, are the same type of force, and are equal in magnitude but opposite in direction.

For example, when you push against a wall, the wall pushes back on you with an equal force. When Earth pulls you downward with gravity, you pull Earth upward with the same gravitational force.

Key Fact

Newton's third law pairs are always the same type of force, act on two different objects, are equal in size, and act in opposite directions.

Inertial mass is a measure of how difficult it is to change the velocity of an object. It is defined as the ratio of force over acceleration:

$$m = \frac{F}{a}$$

An object with a large inertial mass requires a large force to produce even a small acceleration. This is why it is much harder to push a loaded trolley than an empty one.

Circular Motion

An object moving in a circle at constant speed is constantly changing direction, so its velocity is changing. This means the object is accelerating, even though its speed stays the same.

For an object to move in a circle, there must be a resultant force acting towards the centre of the circle. This force is called the centripetal force. Without this force, the object would move in a straight line (Newton's first law). The centripetal force could be provided by tension, gravity, friction, or another force depending on the situation.

Exam Tip: When asked about Newton's laws, always identify the forces involved and state whether the resultant force is zero or not. For F = ma calculations, remember that F is the resultant force, not just any single force. Show your working clearly and include units in every step.

Forces are vector quantities that arise from interactions between objects. Newton's three laws explain how forces affect motion: the first law links zero resultant force to constant velocity, the second law quantifies the relationship \(F = ma\), and the third law states that forces always come in equal and opposite pairs. Understanding free body diagrams and the difference between mass and weight is essential for tackling force calculations in the exam.

glossary_terms.definition: A push or a pull that acts on an object due to the interaction with another object. Forces are measured in newtons (N) and are vector quantities.
A force that acts between objects that are physically touching, such as friction, normal contact force, tension, and air resistance.
A force that acts between objects without them touching, such as gravitational, electrostatic, and magnetic forces.
A quantity that has magnitude (size) only, with no direction. Examples include mass, speed, distance, energy, and temperature.
A quantity that has both magnitude and direction. Examples include force, velocity, displacement, acceleration, and momentum.
A diagram showing all the forces acting on a single object, drawn as arrows from the object. Arrow length represents force magnitude.
The single force that has the same effect as all the individual forces acting on an object combined.
If the resultant force on an object is zero, it stays stationary or moves at constant velocity. If the resultant force is not zero, the object accelerates.
The force of gravity acting on an object, measured in newtons. Weight = mass × gravitational field strength (W = mg).
The force of gravity per unit mass at a point in a gravitational field, measured in N/kg. On Earth, g is approximately 9.8 N/kg.
A measure of how difficult it is to change the velocity of an object. Defined as the ratio of force to acceleration (m = F/a).
The resultant force that acts towards the centre of a circle, keeping an object moving in a circular path.

• Some kinetic energy is transferred to thermal energy / sound during the collision — it is an inelastic collision (1)

• Because the time is very short (0.5 s), the force is very large (1)

before.content_html:
Light as an Electromagnetic Wave

Light is a transverse electromagnetic wave. It is part of the electromagnetic spectrum and travels at approximately \(3 \times 10^8\) m/s in a vacuum. Like all EM waves, light transfers energy from a source to an observer.

When light meets a surface or boundary, it can be reflected, refracted, transmitted, or absorbed. The behaviour depends on the wavelength of the light and the properties of the substance.

Key Fact

When electromagnetic waves meet a boundary between materials, they may be absorbed, transmitted, refracted, or reflected. The way they behave varies with wavelength.

Reflection

When light reflects off a smooth surface (like a plane mirror), it obeys the law of reflection: the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection. Both angles are measured from the normal — an imaginary line perpendicular to the surface at the point where the ray hits.

Smooth surfaces produce specular reflection, giving clear images. Rough surfaces produce diffuse reflection, scattering light in many directions.

To draw a ray diagram for reflection: (1) Draw the mirror as a straight line. (2) Draw the normal at 90° to the surface at the point where the incident ray hits. (3) Draw the incident ray arriving at the surface. (4) Measure the angle of incidence (between the incident ray and the normal). (5) Draw the reflected ray at the same angle on the other side of the normal.

Always use a ruler and protractor in the exam. Label the incident ray, reflected ray, normal, angle of incidence (\(i\)), and angle of reflection (\(r\)).

Refraction

Refraction occurs when light passes from one transparent medium into another (for example, from air into glass). The light changes speed at the boundary. If it hits the boundary at an angle to the normal, it also changes direction.

When light passes from a less dense medium (like air) into a more dense medium (like glass), it slows down and bends towards the normal. When it passes from a more dense medium into a less dense medium, it speeds up and bends away from the normal.

Key Fact

Light bends towards the normal when it slows down (entering a denser medium) and away from the normal when it speeds up (entering a less dense medium). A ray hitting the boundary along the normal passes straight through without bending.

In this core practical, you investigate how light refracts as it enters and exits a rectangular glass block.

Method: Place the glass block on paper and draw around it. Shine a ray of light at different angles into the block using a ray box. Mark the incident ray, the point where it enters the block, the point where it exits, and the emergent ray. Remove the block and draw the refracted ray through the block by joining the entry and exit points.

Key observations: The light bends towards the normal on entering the glass (it slows down) and bends away from the normal on leaving (it speeds up). The emergent ray is parallel to the incident ray but displaced sideways. If the angle of incidence is 0° (along the normal), no bending occurs.

The independent variable is the angle of incidence. The dependent variable is the angle of refraction. Control variables include the same glass block and the same light source.

How EM Waves Interact with Matter

Different substances absorb, transmit, refract, or reflect electromagnetic waves in ways that vary with wavelength. For example, glass transmits visible light but absorbs ultraviolet. The atmosphere transmits visible light and radio waves but absorbs most gamma rays and X-rays.

The differences in velocities of electromagnetic waves in different substances cause refraction. When EM waves pass from one material to another where they travel at a different speed, the change in speed can cause a change in direction.

Changes within atoms and their nuclei can generate electromagnetic radiation across a wide frequency range. For example, when electrons in an atom move from a higher energy level to a lower one, they emit EM radiation — the frequency depends on the energy difference.

Conversely, atoms can absorb EM radiation, causing electrons to move to higher energy levels or, at very high frequencies, causing changes within the nucleus itself. Radio waves can be produced by oscillations in electrical circuits, and can themselves induce oscillations in a receiving circuit.

Key Fact

In the core practical, light bends towards the normal when entering glass (slowing down) and away from the normal when leaving (speeding up). The emergent ray is parallel to the incident ray but displaced sideways.

Measuring the Speed of Waves

The speed of sound in air can be measured by timing an echo over a known distance, or by using two microphones connected to a timer. The speed of ripples on water can be measured using a ripple tank: create waves of known frequency and measure the wavelength using a strobe light or ruler, then calculate speed using \(v = f \times \lambda\).

Exam Tip: In the glass block practical, always draw the normal first, then measure angles from the normal (not from the surface). Remember that the emergent ray comes out parallel to the incident ray. If asked to explain refraction, link the change in direction to the change in speed — do not just say "light bends" without explaining why.

Light is a transverse electromagnetic wave that can be reflected, refracted, transmitted, or absorbed when it meets a boundary. Reflection follows the law of reflection (angle of incidence = angle of reflection). Refraction occurs because light changes speed when moving between media — it bends towards the normal when slowing down and away when speeding up. The core practical with a glass block demonstrates these principles. Different materials interact with EM radiation differently depending on wavelength, and changes in atoms can both generate and absorb electromagnetic radiation.

before.description: Magnets, magnetic fields, electromagnets, the motor effect, and Fleming's left-hand rule.
Electromagnetic induction, transformers, and the National Grid's high-voltage transmission.
before.content_html:
The Motor Effect

When a conductor carrying an electric current is placed in a magnetic field, it experiences a force. This is called the motor effect. The force arises because the magnetic field around the current-carrying wire interacts with the external magnetic field from the permanent magnet. An equal and opposite force also acts on the magnet itself — this is Newton's third law in action.

The motor effect only occurs when the current and the magnetic field are not parallel. The force is greatest when the current is at right angles (perpendicular) to the magnetic field. If the current is parallel to the field, there is no force.

Key Fact

A current-carrying conductor in a magnetic field experiences a force. The direction of this force can be found using Fleming's left-hand rule.

Fleming's Left-Hand Rule

Fleming's left-hand rule allows you to work out the direction of the force (and therefore the direction the conductor moves) when the current and magnetic field directions are known. Hold your left hand so that the thumb, first finger, and second finger are all at right angles to each other:

  • Thumb = direction of the Force (motion)
  • First finger = direction of the magnetic Field (north to south)
  • Second finger = direction of the Current (conventional, positive to negative)

If either the current or the magnetic field direction is reversed, the force reverses too. If both are reversed, the force stays the same.

Calculating the Force on a Conductor

The size of the force on a current-carrying conductor in a magnetic field can be calculated using the equation:

$$F = B \times I \times l$$

Where \(F\) is the force in newtons (N), \(B\) is the magnetic flux density in tesla (T), \(I\) is the current in amperes (A), and \(l\) is the length of the conductor in the field in metres (m).

A wire of length 0.25 m carries a current of 4 A at right angles to a magnetic field of flux density 0.3 T. Calculate the force on the wire.

\(F = B \times I \times l = 0.3 \times 4 \times 0.25 = 0.3\) N

The force on the wire is 0.3 N.

Key Fact

\(F = B \times I \times l\) — force (N) = magnetic flux density (T) × current (A) × length (m). This equation only applies when the current is at right angles to the magnetic field.

How an Electric Motor Works

An electric motor uses the motor effect to produce rotation. A rectangular coil of wire is placed between the poles of a permanent magnet. When current flows through the coil, one side of the coil is pushed up and the other side is pushed down (by Fleming's left-hand rule), making the coil spin.

A split-ring commutator reverses the direction of the current every half turn, ensuring that the forces on each side of the coil continue to push in the same rotational direction. Without the commutator, the coil would stop and reverse after each half turn.

Electromagnetic Induction

Electromagnetic induction is the process of generating a potential difference (and, if the circuit is complete, a current) by moving a conductor through a magnetic field, or by changing the magnetic field around a conductor. This is the principle behind generators and transformers.

The size and direction of the induced potential difference depend on several factors:

  • The speed of movement — faster movement induces a larger potential difference
  • The strength of the magnetic field — a stronger field induces a larger potential difference
  • The number of turns on the coil — more turns induce a larger potential difference
  • The direction of movement or field change — reversing the direction reverses the induced potential difference

The magnetic field produced by the induced current always opposes the original change that caused it. This is known as Lenz's law.

Transformers and the National Grid

A transformer uses electromagnetic induction to change the size of an alternating voltage. It consists of two coils of wire — a primary coil and a secondary coil — wound around a shared iron core. An alternating current in the primary coil creates a changing magnetic field in the iron core, which induces an alternating voltage in the secondary coil.

A step-up transformer has more turns on the secondary coil than the primary, so the output voltage is higher than the input. A step-down transformer has fewer turns on the secondary coil, so the output voltage is lower.

Key Fact

In the national grid, step-up transformers increase the voltage at power stations to reduce the current. Lower current means less energy is wasted as heat in the transmission cables. Step-down transformers then reduce the voltage to safe levels for homes and businesses.

For a 100% efficient transformer, the power input equals the power output. This gives the equation:

$$V_P \times I_P = V_S \times I_S$$

Where \(V_P\) and \(I_P\) are the voltage and current in the primary coil, and \(V_S\) and \(I_S\) are the voltage and current in the secondary coil. If a transformer steps up the voltage, it must step down the current by the same factor (and vice versa), so that power is conserved.

Example: A step-up transformer has a primary voltage of 230 V and a primary current of 10 A. The secondary voltage is 11,500 V. What is the secondary current?

\(V_P \times I_P = V_S \times I_S\)

\(230 \times 10 = 11{,}500 \times I_S\)

\(I_S = \frac{2300}{11500} = 0.2\) A

practice_questions.text: Describe how electromagnetic induction works and explain how this principle is used in a transformer to change the voltage of an alternating supply.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5–6 marks): Clearly explains electromagnetic induction (changing magnetic field induces a p.d. in a conductor). Describes transformer structure (primary/secondary coils, iron core). Explains how alternating current in the primary creates a changing magnetic field that induces a voltage in the secondary. Links number of turns to voltage change. Well-structured.

before.content_html:
Stretching, Bending, and Compressing

When forces act on an object, they can change its shape. An object can be stretched, bent, or compressed. In every case, more than one force is required to change the shape — a single force would simply cause the object to accelerate rather than deform. For example, to stretch a spring you must pull both ends in opposite directions, or fix one end and pull the other.

Key Fact

Stretching, bending, or compressing an object always requires more than one force. A single force would cause acceleration, not deformation.

Elastic and Inelastic Distortion

When a force deforms an object, the deformation can be either elastic distortion or inelastic distortion.

In elastic distortion, the object returns to its original shape and size once the force is removed. A stretched rubber band that springs back to its original length is an example of elastic behaviour. In inelastic distortion, the object is permanently deformed — it does not return to its original shape. Bending a paperclip is an example of inelastic distortion.

A spring behaves elastically as long as it is not stretched beyond its elastic limit. Beyond this point, the spring undergoes inelastic distortion and will not return to its original length when the force is removed.

Hooke’s Law

Hooke’s law states that the extension of a spring is directly proportional to the force applied, as long as the elastic limit is not exceeded. The equation is:

$$F = k \times x$$

Where \(F\) is the force applied in newtons (N), \(k\) is the spring constant in newtons per metre (N/m), and \(x\) is the extension in metres (m).

A stiffer spring has a larger spring constant — it requires more force to produce the same extension. The spring constant can be found by rearranging the equation: \(k = \frac{F}{x}\).

A spring has a spring constant of 40 N/m. Calculate the force needed to extend the spring by 0.15 m.

\(F = k \times x = 40 \times 0.15 = 6\) N

The force needed is 6 N.

Key Fact

Hooke’s law: \(F = k \times x\). The extension is directly proportional to the force, but only up to the elastic limit. Beyond this point, the relationship is no longer linear and the spring does not return to its original length.

Force-Extension Graphs

A force-extension graph shows the relationship between force and extension for a material. For a spring obeying Hooke’s law, the graph is a straight line through the origin — this is a linear relationship. The gradient of the straight-line section equals the spring constant \(k\).

If the spring is stretched beyond its elastic limit, the graph curves — the extension increases more quickly for each additional unit of force. This is a non-linear relationship. The point where the line starts to curve marks the elastic limit.

Different materials produce different shaped graphs. A rubber band, for example, does not obey Hooke’s law — its force-extension graph is curved from the start. It still returns to its original shape (elastic), but the relationship between force and extension is non-linear.

Energy Stored in a Stretched Spring

When a spring is stretched (or compressed) within its elastic limit, work is done on the spring, and energy is stored as elastic potential energy. The amount of energy stored can be calculated using the equation:

$$E = \frac{1}{2} \times k \times x^2$$

Where \(E\) is the energy transferred in stretching (joules, J), \(k\) is the spring constant (N/m), and \(x\) is the extension (m). This equation only applies when the spring obeys Hooke’s law — within the elastic limit.

A spring with a spring constant of 80 N/m is stretched by 0.10 m. Calculate the elastic potential energy stored in the spring.

\(E = \frac{1}{2} \times k \times x^2 = \frac{1}{2} \times 80 \times 0.10^2 = \frac{1}{2} \times 80 \times 0.01 = 0.4\) J

The elastic potential energy stored is 0.4 J.

Key Fact

Elastic potential energy: \(E = \frac{1}{2} k x^2\). This equation applies only when the spring obeys Hooke’s law (within the elastic limit). Notice that energy depends on extension squared — doubling the extension quadruples the energy stored.

Core Practical: Investigating Springs

In this required practical, you investigate the relationship between force and extension for a spring and calculate the work done.

  • Method: Clamp a spring vertically. Measure its natural (unstretched) length with a ruler. Add masses one at a time, recording the new length each time. Calculate the extension (new length minus original length) for each mass.
  • Variables: Independent variable = force (weight of masses). Dependent variable = extension. Control variables = same spring, same starting position, same measuring equipment.
  • Analysis: Plot a force-extension graph. The straight-line region confirms Hooke’s law. The gradient equals the spring constant. If the line curves, the elastic limit has been exceeded.
  • Accuracy: Read the ruler at eye level to avoid parallax error. Wait for the spring to stop oscillating before reading. Repeat readings and calculate a mean to improve reliability.
